🚨🌐 CRITICAL WORDPRESS FLAW LETS UNAUTHENTICATED ATTACKERS TAKE OVER ADMIN ACCOUNTS  CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🔥 Critical Vulnerability · August 24, 2026  🎯 A critical vulnerability affecting the popular WordPress:  🔥 PODS — CUSTOM CONTENT TYPES AND FIELDS  plugin could allow an attacker with:  ❌ NO ACCOUNT  ❌ NO AUTHENTICATION  ❌ NO USER INTERACTION  to escalate privileges all the way to:  🚨 WORDPRESS ADMINISTRATOR.  The vulnerability is:  🔥 CVE-2026-19598  Severity:  🚨 CVSS 9.8 / 10 — CRITICAL  and vulnerable releases include Pods versions up to and including:  ❌ 3.3.9.  The plugin has:  🔥 100,000+ ACTIVE INSTALLATIONS.  ---  ### 🔓 WHAT WENT WRONG?  The issue exists inside a publicly accessible AJAX component called:  pods_admin.  This router is responsible for sending requests toward administrative API functionality.  Normally, several security checks should happen:  🔐 Is the requested function permitted?  👤 Is the requester authenticated?  🎟️ Is the WordPress nonce valid?  🛡️ Does the user have sufficient privileges?  But researchers discovered a dangerous logic problem.  These checks rely on a function called:  pods_error()  to stop processing when something is wrong.  Under a specific JSON compatibility path involving:  meta-box-loader  the function could:  📝 log the error  and return false…  WITHOUT STOPPING EXECUTION.  ---  ### 💥 THE RESULT  The security control effectively says:  ❌ ACCESS DENIED  but the application continues executing anyway.  That means:  authentication check fails ↓ authorization check fails ↓ nonce check fails ↓ error generated ↓ execution continues ↓ privileged API becomes reachable.  This is a classic reminder that:  🚨 DETECTING AN AUTHORIZATION FAILURE  is useless if the application doesn't actually:  🛑 STOP EXECUTION.  ---  ### 👑 ADMIN ACCOUNT TAKEOVER  Researchers found attackers could potentially reach the:  save_user  administrative method.  This could allow an unauthenticated attacker to modify an existing WordPress user's information.  Most critically:  🔥 THE ATTACKER COULD OVERWRITE AN ADMINISTRATOR PASSWORD.  Attack chain:  Internet ↓ vulnerable Pods AJAX endpoint ↓ authorization bypass ↓ save_user ↓ administrator password changed ↓ attacker logs in ↓ FULL WORDPRESS ADMIN ACCESS.  ---  ### 💀 WHAT ADMIN ACCESS CAN BECOME  Once an attacker controls WordPress administrator privileges, they may potentially:  📝 modify website content  👤 create additional administrators  🔌 install malicious plugins  📂 modify files  🐚 deploy web shells  🦠 distribute malware  🎣 inject phishing pages  🔀 redirect visitors  and potentially reach:  🔥 SERVER-SIDE CODE EXECUTION  depending on configuration and available functionality.  So this is not simply:  “someone can modify a WordPress setting.”  It can become:  🌐 COMPLETE SITE COMPROMISE.  ---  ### 📊 AFFECTED VERSIONS  CVE-2026-19598 affects vulnerable releases across multiple Pods branches, including the current 3.3 line through:  ❌ 3.3.9.  Patched releases include:  ✅ 2.8.23.4  ✅ 2.9.19.4  ✅ 3.0.10.4  ✅ 3.1.4.2  ✅ 3.2.8.3  ✅ 3.3.9.1.  Pods released:  🔥 3.3.9.1  on August 14.  ---  ### 🔎 NVD CONFIRMS THE SEVERITY  NIST's National Vulnerability Database describes the issue as:  🔥 CWE-863 — INCORRECT AUTHORIZATION  with:  CVSS 3.1:  🚨 9.8 CRITICAL  Attack vector:  🌐 NETWORK  Attack complexity:  🟢 LOW  Privileges required:  ❌ NONE  User interaction:  ❌ NONE.  That's close to the worst combination possible for an internet-facing application vulnerability.  ---  ### 🛡️ WORDPRESS ADMIN TAKEAWAYS  Site owners should immediately:  ✅ check whether Pods is installed  ✅ identify the exact version  ✅ upgrade to the patched release  ✅ review all administrator accounts  ✅ look for unexpected password changes  ✅ search WordPress and web-server logs  ✅ investigate unusual AJAX requests  ✅ rotate privileged credentials if compromise is suspected  ✅ remove unused administrators  ✅ enforce MFA for privileged users  ✅ ensure WordPress, themes and plugins remain patched.  Do NOT simply assume:  “WordPress auto-update probably handled it.”  Verify.  ---  ### 🧠 WHY IT MATTERS  WordPress vulnerabilities are attractive because one vulnerability can potentially expose:  🌐 thousands of internet-facing websites.  And this bug demonstrates a particularly dangerous failure pattern:  Security checks existed.  Authentication existed.  Authorization existed.  Nonce validation existed.  But one control-flow mistake meant:  🚨 ALL OF THEM COULD BE BYPASSED.  Security isn't only about having checks in the code.  The checks must actually control execution.  Because:  Access denied + execution continues  effectively means:  🔥 ACCESS GRANTED.  🔗 Sources: GBHackers • NIST NVD • Wordfence  #CyberSecurity #WordPress #CVE202619598 #Vulnerability #AppSec #WebSecurity #Wordfence #CriticalVulnerability #PatchNow #SOC #CyberDefense #CyberNews

🚨🔐 CRITICAL CITRIX NETSCALER AUTH BYPASS SCORES 9.3 — INTERNET-FACING GATEWAYS URGED TO PATCH IMMEDIATELY  CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🌐 Network Security · August 24, 2026  🎯 Security researchers are urging organizations to urgently patch a newly disclosed authentication-bypass vulnerability affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway.  The vulnerability:  🔥 CVE-2026-19490  has a:  🚨 CVSS v4 SCORE OF 9.3 / 10  and affects systems frequently deployed directly on the:  🌐 INTERNET-FACING NETWORK PERIMETER.  At the time of the latest reporting:  ✅ no confirmed exploitation had been observed.  But researchers warn that Citrix gateway vulnerabilities historically become attractive targets very quickly.  ---  ### 🔥 WHAT IS CVE-2026-19490?  The vulnerability is classified as:  🔓 AUTHENTICATION BYPASS USING AN ALTERNATE PATH  CWE-288.  Under affected configurations, an attacker may potentially bypass authentication controls protecting a NetScaler Gateway or AAA virtual server.  And that's particularly serious because these systems can provide:  🔐 VPN access  🌐 remote application access  ⚙️ application delivery  📡 traffic management  🛡️ security functions  to enterprise environments.  ---  ### 🌍 WHY NETSCALER IS SUCH A HIGH-VALUE TARGET  NetScaler Gateway often lives exactly where attackers want to attack:  Internet ↓ NetScaler Gateway ↓ authentication ↓ corporate network.  These appliances may expose:  🔐 SSL VPN  🖥️ ICA Proxy  🌐 CVPN  🖥️ RDP Proxy  and other remote-access functions.  That makes authentication bypass especially dangerous.  If authentication is the gate protecting internal access…  a vulnerability that interferes with that gate deserves immediate attention.  ---  ### ⚠️ AFFECTED VERSIONS  Citrix says affected installations include:  ❌ NetScaler ADC / Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-73.32  ❌ NetScaler ADC / Gateway 13.1 before 13.1-63.21  ❌ NetScaler ADC FIPS before 14.1-73.32 FIPS  ❌ NetScaler ADC FIPS / NDcPP before 13.1-37.277.  Secure Private Access Hybrid deployments using vulnerable NetScaler instances can also be affected.  ---  ### 🛠️ PATCHED VERSIONS  Organizations should upgrade to:  ✅ 14.1-73.32 or later  ✅ 13.1-63.21 or later  or the corresponding updated:  🔐 FIPS / NDcPP  builds.  Important:  🚫 CITRIX LISTS NO WORKAROUND.  That means patching is the primary remediation.  ---  ### 🔐 CONFIGURATION MATTERS  Exposure to CVE-2026-19490 depends partly on how the appliance is configured.  Affected scenarios can include NetScaler appliances operating as:  🌐 Gateway  or:  🔐 AAA virtual servers.  For newer affected releases, configurations involving:  🔑 SAML ACTIONS  are particularly relevant.  Administrators should inspect their configuration rather than assuming a NetScaler appliance isn't exposed.  ---  ### 🧨 THERE IS ALSO A SECOND VULNERABILITY  Citrix disclosed another flaw alongside CVE-2026-19490:  ⚠️ CVE-2026-19489  CVSS:  🔥 8.8.  This issue involves a:  🧠 MEMORY OVERFLOW  that may cause:  ❌ unpredictable behavior  or  💥 denial of service.  But CVE-2026-19490 is receiving the most urgent attention because it directly affects authentication.  ---  ### 🚨 NOT EXPLOITED — YET  This distinction matters.  As of August 19:  ❌ Rapid7 had not observed exploitation of CVE-2026-19490 in the wild.  So this is NOT currently a confirmed mass exploitation campaign.  However…  Rapid7 warned organizations to treat patching as an:  🔥 EMERGENCY PRIORITY.  Why?  Because Citrix perimeter products have repeatedly been targeted rapidly after vulnerability disclosure.  Attackers know these appliances can offer something extremely valuable:  🚪 a route into enterprise networks.  ---  ### 🛡️ SOC / BLUE TEAM TAKEAWAYS  Security teams should immediately:  ✅ identify every NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliance  ✅ determine exact software versions  ✅ check whether appliances are internet-facing  ✅ identify Gateway / AAA configurations  ✅ check for SAML configuration  ✅ install patched builds  ✅ review authentication logs  ✅ examine unusual VPN sessions  ✅ review newly created or anomalous accounts  ✅ investigate suspicious external IP access  ✅ monitor vendor and threat-intelligence updates for exploitation.  Because if exploitation begins…  internet-facing NetScaler infrastructure will likely become a high-priority scanning target.  ---  ### 🧠 WHY IT MATTERS  Perimeter vulnerabilities are dangerous because attackers don't necessarily need:  🎣 phishing  🦠 malware attachments  👤 user interaction.  They can potentially attack the system designed to protect the network itself.  And NetScaler appliances are especially sensitive because they often sit directly between:  🌍 THE INTERNET  and  🏢 THE ENTERPRISE.  The vulnerability isn't confirmed as exploited today.  But defenders have something attackers often don't give them:  ⏱️ A PATCHING WINDOW.  The question is whether organizations use it before exploitation begins.  🔗 Sources: Cyber Daily • Citrix / Cloud Software Group • Rapid7  #CyberSecurity #Citrix #NetScaler #CVE202619490 #Vulnerability #NetworkSecurity #VPN #ZeroTrust #SOC #BlueTeam #PatchManagement #CyberDefense #CyberNews

🚨🤖 HACKERS ARE ACTIVELY EXPLOITING A CRITICAL MLFLOW FLAW TO HUNT FOR CLOUD CREDENTIALS  CyberSignal Daily ✓ · ☁️ AI Infrastructure Security · August 24, 2026  🎯 Security teams running MLflow are being urged to patch immediately after attackers were observed exploiting a critical vulnerability in the popular open-source AI engineering platform.  The vulnerability:  🔥 CVE-2026-64849  affects:  ❌ MLflow versions before 3.15.0  and involves an:  🚨 UNAUTHENTICATED SERVER-SIDE REQUEST FORGERY — SSRF  vulnerability.  This isn't just a theoretical flaw.  Researchers say:  ⚠️ ACTIVE EXPLOITATION HAS ALREADY BEEN OBSERVED.  And the attackers appear particularly interested in something extremely valuable:  🔑 CLOUD CREDENTIALS 🔐 SECRETS ☁️ INTERNAL METADATA SERVICES.  ---  ### 🤖 WHAT IS MLFLOW?  MLflow is an open-source AI engineering platform used to build and manage:  🧠 machine-learning models 🤖 AI agents 💬 LLM applications 📊 experiments 📦 model registries.  The platform says it is used by thousands of organizations.  That makes vulnerabilities affecting exposed MLflow infrastructure especially interesting to attackers.  ---  ### 🔥 THE VULNERABILITY  The vulnerable component involves MLflow's:  🔗 MODEL REGISTRY WEBHOOKS.  Specifically, the endpoint:  POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test  could be abused without authentication in affected default deployments.  MLflow attempted to validate the destination of webhook requests.  But researchers discovered a weakness:  The software validated the:  ✅ INITIAL URL  but could then follow:  ➡️ HTTP REDIRECTS  without properly validating the new destination.  That creates an SSRF bypass.  The attack can effectively become:  Attacker ↓ MLflow webhook endpoint ↓ attacker-controlled URL ↓ HTTP redirect ↓ internal service / cloud metadata endpoint ↓ MLflow fetches data ↓ response returned to attacker.  ---  ### ☁️ WHY CLOUD ENVIRONMENTS ARE PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS  Cloud systems often expose metadata services internally.  Those services may contain information related to:  🔑 temporary credentials  🪪 IAM identities  ⚙️ instance configuration  ☁️ cloud environment metadata.  An external attacker normally shouldn't be able to communicate directly with those internal endpoints.  But SSRF can turn the vulnerable MLflow server into a:  🔥 PROXY INSIDE THE NETWORK.  Researchers warned attackers could potentially target addresses associated with internal cloud services.  If sensitive credentials are returned…  the attack may evolve from:  MLflow vulnerability  into:  ☁️ CLOUD COMPROMISE.  ---  ### 🎯 ATTACKERS ARE ALREADY LOOKING FOR SECRETS  According to threat intelligence cited by Cyber Daily, honeypot telemetry has observed attackers abusing CVE-2026-64849 against cloud-hosted MLflow systems.  Their apparent objective:  🔎 identify internal services  and attempt to extract:  🔑 credentials 🔐 secrets.  That means defenders should not treat this as:  “Patch when convenient.”  The exploitation window has already opened.  ---  ### 💥 WHAT COULD HAPPEN AFTER CREDENTIAL THEFT?  The SSRF itself may only be the beginning.  If an attacker retrieves credentials associated with an overly privileged cloud identity, the attack chain could become:  CVE-2026-64849 ↓ SSRF ↓ cloud metadata request ↓ credentials/secrets retrieved ↓ cloud environment enumeration ↓ access to storage/workloads ↓ lateral movement ↓ data theft.  Depending on the privileges attached to the compromised identity, attackers could potentially access:  🪣 cloud storage  🔐 additional secrets  🖥️ workloads  📊 sensitive datasets  ⚙️ cloud-management APIs.  ---  ### 🛡️ CISA HAS ALSO FLAGGED THE VULNERABILITY  CVE-2026-64849 was added to the:  🔥 CISA KNOWN EXPLOITED VULNERABILITIES — KEV  catalog on August 19.  That designation is important.  CISA's KEV catalog focuses on vulnerabilities with evidence of real-world exploitation.  ---  ### ✅ THE FIX  Organizations should upgrade MLflow to:  🔥 VERSION 3.15.0 OR LATER.  Version 3.15.0 introduces stronger SSRF protections designed to validate the actual connection destination, including destinations reached through redirects.  Organizations should also investigate whether vulnerable MLflow instances were:  🌐 internet-facing  and whether suspicious requests occurred before patching.  ---  ### 🔎 SOC / BLUE TEAM CHECKLIST  Defenders running MLflow should urgently:  ✅ inventory all MLflow instances  ✅ identify versions below 3.15.0  ✅ patch exposed systems immediately  ✅ inspect webhook activity  ✅ search HTTP logs for unusual requests to webhook endpoints  ✅ investigate traffic toward cloud metadata IP addresses  ✅ rotate potentially exposed credentials  ✅ review IAM permissions  ✅ enforce least privilege  ✅ restrict MLflow management interfaces from unnecessary internet exposure.  Teams should pay particular attention to requests involving internal destinations such as:  169.254.169.254  which is commonly associated with cloud instance metadata services.  ---  ### 🧠 WHY IT MATTERS  AI infrastructure is rapidly becoming part of enterprise production environments.  But that also means tools originally used by:  👨‍💻 developers 📊 data scientists 🤖 ML engineers  are becoming part of the organization's:  🔥 SECURITY PERIMETER.  An exposed MLflow server isn't simply an “AI development tool” anymore.  If it can reach:  ☁️ cloud infrastructure 🔑 credentials 🗄️ internal services  then compromising it may provide attackers with a bridge into much more sensitive systems.  The attack chain is becoming clear:  AI infrastructure ↓ vulnerability ↓ SSRF ↓ cloud metadata ↓ credentials ↓ potential broader compromise.  As organizations race to deploy AI…  attackers are increasingly learning how to attack the infrastructure underneath it.  🔗 Sources: Cyber Daily • NVD • GitHub Security Advisory • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security  #CyberSecurity #MLflow #CVE202664849 #AIsecurity #CloudSecurity #Vulnerability #CISA #AppSec #ThreatIntelligence #SOC #BlueTeam #CyberDefense #CyberNews

💀💰 RANSOMWARE ATTACKERS ARE ZEROING IN ON MID-MARKET COMPANIES — 73% OF DISCLOSED INCIDENTS FALL INTO THIS SEGMENT  CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🧨 Ransomware · August 24, 2026  🎯 A new analysis from Black Kite highlights a major reality about modern ransomware:  Attackers aren't only hunting billion-dollar corporations.  They're heavily targeting the companies sitting in the middle.  🔥 MID-MARKET ORGANIZATIONS  accounted for:  📊 73%  of publicly disclosed ransomware and data-extortion incidents with known company revenue across North America and Europe between:  📅 January 2023 and 📅 June 2026.  The analysis covered:  🔥 13,336 INCIDENTS  with known victim revenue.  Black Kite defined mid-market companies as businesses generating between:  💰 $10 MILLION  and  💰 $1 BILLION  in annual revenue.  And the proportion wasn't a temporary spike.  Throughout the analyzed period, mid-market victims consistently represented roughly:  📊 72%–75%  of ransomware and extortion incidents.  ---  ### 💰 THE SMALLEST MID-MARKET COMPANIES ARE HIT HARDEST  More than half of the mid-market victims generated only:  💵 $10M–$50M  in annual revenue.  That makes this group particularly attractive.  Why?  Because they may have:  💰 valuable data  🌐 significant infrastructure  🤝 connections to larger enterprises  📦 supply-chain access  but often lack the:  👥 security staffing  💵 cybersecurity budgets  🛡️ defensive maturity  of very large enterprises.  For ransomware operators, that can create an attractive balance between:  VALUE + ACCESSIBILITY.  ---  ### 🏭 MANUFACTURING TAKES THE BIGGEST HIT  Manufacturing represented:  🔥 MORE THAN ONE-QUARTER  of the observed mid-market ransomware victims.  Other heavily affected areas included:  🧪 professional, scientific & technical services  🏗️ construction.  Manufacturing is particularly valuable to ransomware operators because operational disruption can immediately affect:  🏭 production  🚚 logistics  📦 deliveries  🤝 suppliers  💰 revenue.  Downtime gives attackers leverage.  ---  ### 🚨 THE EXPOSURE NUMBERS ARE SERIOUS  Researchers assessed more than:  🔥 120,000 MID-MARKET ORGANIZATIONS.  Among them:  ⚠️ 54.7%  had at least one significant patch-management problem affecting a:  🌐 PUBLIC-FACING SYSTEM.  Even more concerning:  MORE THAN ONE-QUARTER  had a vulnerability already known to be:  🔥 EXPLOITED BY ATTACKERS.  That means many organizations aren't merely carrying theoretical vulnerabilities.  They're exposing weaknesses attackers already know how to weaponize.  ---  ### 🔑 STOLEN CREDENTIALS ARE ANOTHER MAJOR ENTRY POINT  Nearly:  🔥 ONE-THIRD  of monitored organizations had at least one:  🦠 STEALER-LOG FINDING.  Stealer logs are collections of credentials and other information harvested by infostealer malware.  Those stolen credentials can give criminals access to:  📧 email accounts  ☁️ cloud platforms  🌐 VPNs  🖥️ internal systems  🔑 business applications.  The ransomware chain may therefore look like:  Infostealer infection ↓ credentials stolen ↓ credentials sold/traded ↓ initial-access actor obtains access ↓ lateral movement ↓ data theft ↓ ransomware/extortion.  The company initially infected by an infostealer may not realize that those credentials could later become the entrance point for a much larger incident.  ---  ### 🔗 SUPPLY CHAINS MAKE THE PROBLEM BIGGER  Mid-market organizations rarely operate alone.  They frequently provide:  💻 software  📦 products  ☁️ services  🔧 technology  📊 data processing  to much larger organizations.  That means compromising one mid-sized vendor can potentially expose:  ➡️ customers  ➡️ partners  ➡️ suppliers  ➡️ enterprise networks.  A security weakness in a $30 million vendor can therefore become a security problem for a multibillion-dollar customer.  ---  ### 😬 AND VENDOR-RISK TEAMS ARE STRETCHED  One example highlighted in the analysis described a typical vendor-risk team consisting of:  👥 TWO PEOPLE  responsible for more than:  🏢 300 SUPPLIERS.  That illustrates the problem.  Organizations increasingly depend on huge third-party ecosystems…  while the teams responsible for understanding those dependencies may be extremely small.  And some software and services may not even appear in formal vendor inventories.  ---  ### 🤖 AI ADDS ANOTHER DIMENSION  AI is accelerating:  🔎 vulnerability discovery  📊 security-data analysis  🧠 attack research.  Defenders can use AI to find weaknesses faster.  But attackers have access to many of the same capabilities.  That creates increasing pressure on organizations already struggling with:  📚 thousands of vulnerabilities  👥 limited personnel  ⏱️ limited remediation time.  The objective therefore cannot simply be:  “Patch everything immediately.”  Security teams need to prioritize:  🔥 internet-facing systems  🔥 actively exploited vulnerabilities  🔥 exposed credentials  🔥 critical assets  🔥 high-risk suppliers.  ---  ### 🛡️ SOC / BLUE TEAM TAKEAWAYS  For mid-market defenders, the priorities are increasingly clear:  🔎 continuously inventory internet-facing assets  🚨 prioritize known-exploited vulnerabilities  🔑 monitor credentials appearing in stealer logs  🩹 reduce patch-management delays  🔐 strengthen MFA and identity controls  📊 prioritize vulnerabilities based on actual exploitability  🤝 continuously evaluate third-party exposure  💾 maintain tested offline/immutable backups  🧠 monitor ransomware initial-access techniques  🚨 build incident-response procedures BEFORE an attack occurs.  ---  ### 🧠 WHY IT MATTERS  Ransomware economics have evolved.  Attackers don't necessarily need one:  💰 $10 BILLION CORPORATION.  They can attack dozens of:  🏢 $10M–$50M businesses  with weaker defenses.  Automation, stolen credentials, vulnerability scanners and ransomware-as-a-service infrastructure make that strategy increasingly scalable.  And mid-market organizations occupy a dangerous position:  Big enough to possess valuable data.  Big enough to pay.  Connected enough to provide supply-chain access.  But sometimes…  not big enough to maintain enterprise-scale security teams.  That's why the mid-market may increasingly represent one of the most important ransomware battlegrounds.  🔗 Sources: Help Net Security • Black Kite  #CyberSecurity #Ransomware #CyberAttack #ThreatIntelligence #VulnerabilityManagement #Infostealer #SupplyChainSecurity #SOC #BlueTeam #CyberDefense #CyberNews

🚁🔐 AMAZON’S DRONE DELIVERY EXPANSION RAISES NEW CYBERSECURITY & PRIVACY QUESTIONS  CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🛰️ Cyber-Physical Security · August 24, 2026  🎯 Amazon is preparing one of the largest commercial drone-delivery expansions attempted in the United States.  Its Prime Air network is expected to expand to:  🔥 NEARLY 500 U.S. CITIES AND TOWNS  by the end of 2026 — roughly a sixfold increase from its current footprint.  But as thousands of autonomous aircraft potentially become part of everyday logistics, another question becomes increasingly important:  🔐 How do you secure a massive fleet of autonomous, connected flying systems?  Prime Air currently operates from 11 U.S. locations across 10 metropolitan areas, with Amazon preparing additional launches around:  📍 Chicago 📍 Cleveland 📍 Atlanta 📍 Syracuse 📍 Boise  Amazon says it has already completed hundreds of thousands of drone deliveries this year.  The company's highly autonomous drones combine:  📷 onboard cameras 📡 sensors 🛰️ navigation technology 🤖 autonomous decision-making ☁️ backend/cloud infrastructure 🛩️ Detect-and-Avoid systems  to navigate airspace, identify obstacles and determine whether a delivery location is safe.  Amazon says its onboard cameras and sensors are used for navigation, obstacle detection and delivery safety.  According to the company:  🔒 cameras do not track individuals 🎥 there is no live camera feed watched by employees 💻 camera data is processed onboard for navigation.  But large-scale deployment of autonomous connected aircraft also creates an interesting cybersecurity discussion.  Because these aren't simply flying delivery boxes.  They are effectively:  🤖 autonomous robots + 📡 wireless systems + 📷 computer vision + 🛰️ navigation + ☁️ connected infrastructure + ⚙️ physical control systems.  That combination creates a new class of cyber-physical infrastructure that defenders may eventually need to protect at significant scale.  ### ⚠️ POTENTIAL CYBERSECURITY ATTACK SURFACE  As commercial drone fleets become larger, security teams will need to consider several areas.  ### 1️⃣ COMMAND-AND-CONTROL INFRASTRUCTURE  Drone fleets depend on backend systems for operations, flight coordination and delivery workflows.  That makes systems such as:  🔐 credentials 🌐 APIs ☁️ cloud infrastructure 🖥️ fleet-management platforms  important security boundaries.  Compromise of the infrastructure managing autonomous systems could potentially have consequences extending beyond stolen data into the physical world.  ---  ### 2️⃣ NAVIGATION & SENSOR INTEGRITY  Autonomous drones depend heavily on environmental and positional information.  That makes the integrity of:  🛰️ positioning data 📷 visual information 📡 communications 📊 telemetry 🧠 autonomous decision systems  critical.  Manipulating the information consumed by autonomous systems is therefore an important threat category for future cyber-physical infrastructure.  ---  ### 3️⃣ SOFTWARE SUPPLY-CHAIN SECURITY  Modern drones are complex software platforms.  Their ecosystem can include:  📦 third-party libraries ⚙️ firmware ☁️ cloud services 🔄 software updates 🤖 AI/computer-vision components.  A vulnerability introduced somewhere in that chain could potentially propagate across a large fleet.  This makes:  ✅ signed updates ✅ dependency monitoring ✅ secure firmware ✅ vulnerability management ✅ software provenance  extremely important.  ---  ### 4️⃣ CAMERA & SENSOR PRIVACY  Prime Air requires cameras and sensors to understand its environment.  Amazon says those cameras are used for navigation rather than surveillance and that no employee watches a live feed.  Still, widespread drone deployment creates broader privacy questions:  🔎 What information is processed?  💾 What information could be retained?  ☁️ Where is telemetry stored?  🔐 Who can access operational data?  🛡️ How is that information protected?  Privacy and cybersecurity become closely connected when autonomous systems continuously interact with residential environments.  ---  ### 5️⃣ DRONE AUTHENTICATION  Another future security challenge is identification.  Imagine neighborhoods eventually containing drones operated by:  📦 Amazon 🍔 food-delivery companies 🏪 retailers 🚚 logistics providers 🏥 medical-delivery services.  Defenders and regulators may increasingly need mechanisms capable of establishing:  WHO owns the drone?  WHO authorized its flight?  IS its software legitimate?  IS it communicating with legitimate infrastructure?  Because once legitimate commercial drones become normal, malicious or unauthorized aircraft may theoretically attempt to blend into normal drone traffic.  Security experts discussing Amazon's expansion have raised this possibility.  This remains a:  ⚠️ FUTURE RISK SCENARIO  —not evidence that Amazon's drone network has been compromised.  ---  ### 6️⃣ CYBER-PHYSICAL CONSEQUENCES  This may be the most important distinction.  Traditional cyberattacks often affect:  💾 data 🖥️ computers 🌐 networks.  Autonomous systems can introduce another dimension:  🌍 THE PHYSICAL WORLD.  If a vulnerability affects a computer, the result might be:  ❌ application failure.  If a vulnerability affects an autonomous aircraft, the consequences could theoretically include:  ❌ navigation disruption ❌ incorrect behavior ❌ delivery failure ❌ physical safety risks.  That makes cybersecurity inseparable from safety engineering.  ---  ### 🧠 WHY IT MATTERS  There is currently **no evidence in this reporting that Amazon Prime Air has suffered a cyberattack**.  That's important.  The cybersecurity story isn't:  ❌ "Amazon drones have been hacked."  It's:  ⚠️ "Autonomous drone infrastructure is rapidly scaling, and that creates another cyber-physical attack surface that will need to be secured."  Amazon plans to move from 11 current U.S. operating locations toward service covering nearly:  🔥 500 CITIES AND TOWNS  before the end of 2026.  That means autonomous delivery could eventually become another major connected infrastructure layer alongside:  🚘 connected vehicles 🏭 industrial IoT 🤖 autonomous robots 🏠 smart homes 📹 connected surveillance systems.  And cybersecurity teams have learned the same lesson repeatedly:  The more physical infrastructure becomes software-defined and connected…  the more cybersecurity becomes part of physical safety.  The future of delivery may therefore require more than:  📦 fast logistics.  It will require:  🔐 strong authentication 🛡️ secure software supply chains 📡 protected communications ⚙️ hardened autonomous systems 🔎 continuous vulnerability research 👁️ privacy safeguards 🚨 cyber-physical incident response.  Because when software begins flying over our cities…  cybersecurity doesn't stay inside the computer anymore.  🔗 Sources: Yahoo Tech • Amazon Prime Air • Reuters • Techstrong  #CyberSecurity #Amazon #PrimeAir #DroneSecurity #CyberPhysicalSecurity #IoTSecurity #CloudSecurity #Privacy #AutonomousSystems #SupplyChainSecurity #CyberDefense #CyberNews

CYBERGUERRE : L’IA NE VA PAS SEULEMENT AUTOMATISER LES ENTREPRISES. ELLE COMMENCE À AUTOMATISER L’ATTAQUE.  Taïwan : jusqu’à 8 agents IA parallèles, 21 systèmes cartographiés, 85 comptes compromis, puis sûreté nucléaire + 7 groupes énergétiques.  LE COÛT DE L’OFFENSIVE S’EFFONDRE. PAS CELUI DE DÉFENDRE CHAQUE PORTE.  Des attaquants ont utilisé des frameworks d’agents open source pour conduire une intrusion largement automatisée contre des systèmes gouvernementaux taïwanais.  Le coût marginal de l’attaque informatique vient potentiellement de s’effondrer. Avant : 1 hacker → quelques cibles. Demain : 1 opérateur → 8 agents → dizaines de systèmes simultanément. Donc la même logique Jevons revient encore : **CYBERATTACK COST ↓ → NUMBER OF ATTACKS ↑↑**  La défense doit protéger chaque système. L’attaquant n’a besoin que d’en trouver un mauvais. C’est asymétrique.  LA FRANCE MONTRE LA VULNÉRABILITÉ. TAÏWAN MONTRE CE QUI ARRIVE QUAND ON INDUSTRIALISE SON EXPLOITATION.  Aujourd’hui : identifiant compromis → attaquant humain → exploration → exfiltration. Demain : identifiant compromis → 8, 50 ou 500 agents → exploration parallèle → rebond automatique → exfiltration.  C'est potentiellement un changement d'échelle considérable. D'ailleurs après l'attaque de la DGFiP, le gouvernement français a annoncé vouloir employer des outils d'IA souverains, notamment français, pour tester automatiquement les vulnérabilités des services de l'État.  Donc nous avons presque simultanément : TAÏWAN IA utilisée pour automatiser l'offensive. FRANCE IA envisagée pour automatiser la recherche défensive de vulnérabilités.  LA CYBERSÉCURITÉ ENTRE ELLE AUSSI DANS LA COURSE À L’ACCÉLÉRATION. Attaque : agent → découvre → teste → pivote → recommence. Défense : agent → scanne → détecte → corrige → recommence. Et le facteur décisif devient encore une fois : LE TEMPS.  Qui découvre la vulnérabilité le premier ?

🇺🇸 Massachusetts Town Confirms Cyberattack Behind Four-Day Network Outage  The Town of Andover, Massachusetts, has confirmed that a cyberattack caused a multi-day network outage earlier this month, disrupting municipal systems and Andover Public Schools services.  * The incident was first detected on August 13, 2026  * Officials initially described the disruption publicly as a temporary internet connectivity issue  * Town Manager Andrew Flanagan has now confirmed that the outage was caused by a cyberattack  * Andover temporarily took external email offline as part of its response  * Established cyber incident-response procedures were activated  * Independent cybersecurity specialists were brought in to investigate the attack and assist with system restoration  * The disruption affected municipal online services and delayed Andover Public Schools' release of teacher assignments to families  * Most affected systems had been restored by August 17  * Town buildings remained open throughout the incident  * Telephone services continued operating  * Public safety agencies, utilities and other critical infrastructure were reportedly NOT interrupted  ⚠️ Several important questions remain unanswered:  * The threat actor has not been identified  * The initial access vector remains unknown  * Officials have not said whether ransomware or other malware was involved  * It remains unclear whether municipal or school data was accessed, copied or exfiltrated  * The investigation remains ongoing  ⚠️ Analyst Note:  This incident is another reminder that cyberattacks against local governments can create significant operational disruption even when emergency and critical infrastructure services remain available.  At this stage, this should be described as a confirmed cyberattack — NOT a confirmed ransomware or data-breach incident.  Any claims regarding data theft, ransomware attribution or a specific threat actor should remain unverified until Andover or investigators provide additional evidence. This is not in the AI book, but it is in Practive Security 101:  From 2015-2021 as a Principal Engineer and later Sr. Manager, I served as the leader of threat intelligence for Palo Alto Networks. I’ve led threat intel programs for much of my career.  It was toward the end of my time at Palo that the founder of the company along with the product marketing team began saying cyber adversaries and nation states had adopted AI and were using it in ways that overwhelmed existing defenses. They were making the claim that AI gave the adversary the advantage, and so defenders needed to AI all things to counter this.  They had no evidence of this, despite my direct requests for intel that proved it true. I always thought it odd that such claims were being made while those actually researching the adversary, saw no indication this was true. And my charter was defense of the company, so I had reason and right to know. But no one could give me evidence.  Fast forward to my tenure at CrowdStrike, where the weaponization of AI was all over marketing, but again, working with the internal threat intel teams I found no examples and no evidence this was true. We all took it at as marketing.  In fact, earlier this year (2026), I reviewed all the AI attributed threat reports published by Palo Alto and CrowdStrike and found that none of them showed evidence that AI was providing a strategic advantage for the adversary. I published my analysis, using the unchanged MITRE ATT&CK matrix as a key anchor, on the Substack.  We are seeing the weaponization of AI, and there are lots of examples of that. But so far, most of the AI related attacks are actually attacks against AI infrastructure. So I remain unconvinced of the narrative. Partially because I know it started as a lie, and also because I have seen no evidence.  So far, cyber attacks that use AI seem to be using it as an aid via automation and speed and scale, but when it comes down to TTPs…no material changes have been made known yet.  Yes, I know AI is finding new vulnerabilities, but as I have described in videos on the channel, that alone doesn’t mean much.

🚨🤖 Chinese-speaking cybercrime group uses AI to scale attacks against Windows and Linux servers  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · Threat Intelligence · August 24, 2026**  A cybercrime group tracked as **UAT-10147** is showing what AI-assisted offensive operations look like when they move beyond generating a few scripts.  Cisco Talos says the group is using AI-supported workflows across exploitation, reconnaissance, troubleshooting and post-compromise activity while targeting exposed **Windows IIS and Linux web servers** around the world.  The objective appears primarily financial: **data theft and SEO fraud**.  But the tooling behind the operation is considerably more advanced than that description might suggest.  ### 🔎 What happened?  Talos identified UAT-10147 in early 2026 after investigating compromised servers communicating with attacker-controlled infrastructure.  Victims were observed across:  • government • education • media • technology • gaming  and in countries including Brazil, Bolivia, Canada, China and Vietnam.  One attacker-controlled directory also exposed a target list containing approximately:  **170,000 URLs**  suggesting the operation was designed for scale.  Rather than manually handling every target, the attackers appear to automate large portions of the intrusion process.  That is where AI becomes particularly interesting.  ### 🤖 Where AI enters the attack chain  Talos observed UAT-10147 using offensive frameworks and AI-assisted tooling to help with tasks such as:  • vulnerability reconnaissance • exploit generation and refinement • payload creation • exploit validation • troubleshooting • persistence workflows • operational documentation  The actor was also observed using tools including **PentestGPT, DeepAudit, Metasploit and ysoserial**.  In one workflow, AI tooling helped generate malicious Java deserialization payloads alongside scripts for checking writable paths, deploying implants and validating whether exploitation worked correctly.  This isn't the same as saying:  **“AI autonomously hacked 170,000 servers.”**  There is still a human-operated intrusion campaign behind the activity.  But Talos assesses that AI is reducing the expertise and manual effort required to conduct complex attacks at scale.  ### ⚙️ What happens after compromise?  The attack normally begins by exploiting known vulnerabilities in exposed web servers to achieve remote code execution.  From there, the chain can branch depending on the target.  A simplified Windows path looks like:  **Vulnerable web server** ↓ Remote code execution ↓ Privilege escalation ↓ Windows Defender exclusions modified ↓ Malware / web shell deployed ↓ Persistence established ↓ Credential theft / SEO fraud / further access  Talos observed tools including:  **QuasarRAT** **Gh0stCringe** **BadIIS** and a newly analyzed implant called **SPECTRE**.  ### 🧬 SPECTRE is the more serious part of the story  SPECTRE is a custom cross-platform backdoor written in C with versions for both:  🪟 Windows 🐧 Linux  Its capabilities include:  • command-and-control • process injection • credential theft • anti-analysis checks • persistence • defense evasion  The Windows version evaluates its environment for indicators of analysis or sandboxing, including:  RAM CPU count disk capacity processes hostnames usernames sleep behavior  If enough suspicious indicators are detected, the malware can terminate itself rather than expose its behavior to researchers.  ### 🛡️ EDR evasion goes deeper  UAT-10147 also uses **BYOVD — Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver** techniques.  The idea is to introduce a legitimate but vulnerable kernel driver and abuse it to interfere with security products from a highly privileged position.  On Linux, researchers found another component:  **Specter — a kernel-level rootkit.**  Talos believes, with medium confidence, that development of parts of this rootkit involved a combination of:  **AI assistance + human expertise.**  That distinction matters.  The research does not show AI independently inventing an advanced rootkit from scratch.  It shows threat actors increasingly using AI as an engineering accelerator inside an already capable malware-development workflow.  ### 📊 What we know  ✅ UAT-10147 is assessed by Talos as a Chinese-speaking, financially motivated intrusion group.  ✅ It targets internet-facing Windows and Linux servers.  ✅ Talos found an attacker target list containing roughly **170,000 URLs**.  ✅ AI-assisted workflows were observed in exploitation, validation and post-compromise operations.  ✅ SPECTRE works across Windows and Linux.  ✅ The actor also uses BadIIS, QuasarRAT, Gh0stCringe, Meterpreter and Noodle RAT.  ✅ Kernel-level defense evasion has been observed.  ⚠️ This does **not** mean all 170,000 listed URLs were successfully compromised.  The list represents targeting infrastructure — not a confirmed victim count.  ### 🛡️ What defenders should do  Organizations running public web infrastructure should prioritize:  ✅ aggressively patching internet-facing IIS and Linux services  ✅ minimizing unnecessary external exposure  ✅ monitoring unexpected web-shell creation  ✅ watching for Defender exclusion modifications  ✅ hunting for suspicious scheduled tasks  ✅ detecting unusual privilege-escalation tooling  ✅ monitoring driver installation and BYOVD behavior  ✅ alerting on unexpected kernel modules and rootkit indicators  ✅ separating public web infrastructure from sensitive internal systems  The larger defensive lesson is to focus less on whether an attack was “AI-powered” and more on what AI changes operationally:  **speed, scale and attacker consistency.**  ### 🧠 Why it matters  The most important development here isn't a magical autonomous hacker.  It's industrialization.  A relatively capable attacker can increasingly use AI to:  find targets → understand vulnerabilities → generate or modify exploitation code → troubleshoot failures → validate results → document procedures → repeat the process.  That lowers the amount of human attention required per target.  The techniques themselves — RCE, web shells, credential theft, rootkits and EDR bypass — aren't new.  What changes is the economics.  If AI allows one operator to behave more like a larger intrusion team, defenders may face **more capable attacks at much higher volume**.  That may be one of the most consequential ways AI changes cybersecurity.  🔗 **Sources:** Cisco Talos · The Hacker News  #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #AISecurity #Malware

🚨 مجموعة RipperSec تنشر ادعاءً بالوصول إلى نظام إدارة وقود (OPW Fuel Management) في أيرلندا 🇮🇪  🔹 بحسب المنشور: • مقطع فيديو يعرض تنقلاً فعلياً بين تبويبات واجهة النظام في 10 أغسطس 2026  • الظاهر في الواجهة: تبويبات Inventory وSensor وCalendar وList وReports وSettings، مع موقع يضم ثمانية خزانات  • سجل إنذارات لعدة خزانات  • النظام في Normal Mode   🔹 ملاحظات: • الواجهة تبدو أصيلة، ووجود سجل إنذارات ممتد لأسابيع يتسق مع موقع تشغيلي فعلي  • المعروض تصفّح فقط. لا تنفيذ أمر، ولا تعديل قيمة، ولا ما يثبت صلاحية كتابة  • لكن وجود تبويب Settings وأزرار Send All ضمن الواجهة يعني أن الحساب المستخدم قد يملك صلاحيات تهيئة، وهذا غير مُثبت في المقطع  🔎 حدود الأثر: أنظمة قياس مخزون الوقود توفر قراءات وإنذارات، ولا تتحكم مباشرة في الضخ أو التعبئة. الأثر الأسوأ المتصور يتعلق بالتلاعب بحدود الإنذار أو إخفاء تسرّب، لا بإحداث تدفق مباشر  🔎 لا يوجد تأكيد مستقل ولا تحديد للجهة المشغّلة، ولا ما يدل على وصول يتجاوز العرض

🚨 مجموعة RipperSec تنشر ادعاءً بالوصول إلى نظام SCADA لشركة Elicom السويدية 🇸🇪  🔹 بحسب المنشور: • مقطع فيديو يعرض واجهة HMI بالسويدية لنظام سيلو تجفيف حبوب (Torksilo)  • الظاهر في الواجهة: قراءات حرارة ورطوبة للهواء الداخل والخارج والخارجي، وخلاط، ومروحة، وغلاية، وصفحات للإعدادات وبيانات التشغيل  🔹 ملاحظات: • الواجهة تبدو أصيلة، والتسميات السويدية والبنية متسقة مع نظام تجفيف حقيقي  • خلافاً للادعاءات السابقة، المعروض هنا ليس عرضاً فقط. ظهر تعديل فعلي لقيم setpoints في صفحة الإعدادات: حدّان من حدود حماية الغلاية تغيّرا من 100.0% إلى 0.0%  • وظهرت كذلك محاولة إدخال قيمة رُفضت برسالة تحقق من النظام، وهذا بحد ذاته مؤشر على صلاحية كتابة، لا قراءة فقط  🔎 حدود الأثر: نظام تجفيف حبوب لدى مزوّد خدمة. لا خدمة عامة ولا سلامة أرواح. الأثر الأسوأ المتصور يتعلق بتعطيل دورة التجفيف أو إتلاف المحصول إن استمر التلاعب بحدود التشغيل  🔎 لا يوجد تأكيد مستقل ولا رد من الجهة، ولا يُعرف إن كان الوصول لنظام إنتاج فعلي أم وحدة عرض/اختبار.

The flaw reportedly involves insecure deserialization and allows a low-privileged, authenticated domain user to execute arbitrary code over the network against a domain-joined Veeam backup server. Successful exploitation can result in SYSTEM-level control of the server, making the vulnerability particularly significant because backup infrastructure often provides access to sensitive data and recovery operations. The report gives the vulnerability a CVSS score of 9.4 and compares it with earlier Veeam deserialization vulnerabilities, including CVE-2024-40711.  The Lynx ransomware group allegedly claimed to use a private or improved version of the vulnerability that does not require domain credentials. An underground forum advertisement similarly claimed to offer an exploit that bypasses the June 2026 patch and achieves unauthenticated SYSTEM-level remote code execution. As of mid-August 2026, these claims had not been independently verified. The report notes that there was no public technical analysis, confirmed exploitation evidence, or vendor acknowledgment demonstrating a genuine unauthenticated bypass or residual vulnerability. The claims may therefore represent negotiation tactics intended to increase ransom demands or protect an alleged exploit.  The report also connects the vulnerability to a private exploit advertised in 2025, assessing that it may have been an early version of, or the same underlying issue as, CVE-2026-44963. Veeam has historically been targeted by ransomware groups, including Akira, Fog, Cuba, and FIN7, because compromising backup servers enables attackers to disrupt recovery operations before deploying ransomware.  Another major Veeam attack vector is CVE-2023-27532, which can expose credentials from the Veeam backup service and database. Attackers may use these credentials for initial access or lateral movement, including through post-compromise credential-dumping activity. Regardless of whether the alleged unauthenticated exploit exists, the authenticated RCE described for CVE-2026-44963 presents a serious risk wherever domain accounts or backup infrastructure are compromised.

sample_tweets.text: Exactly. Now we're finally at the actual issue.  AIVD upstream. FBI/NSA dissemination. Hawkins downstream from that intelligence. Tamene downstream from Hawkins. CrowdStrike downstream from the DNC.  And the exact selectors connecting those stages remain classified.  So CrowdStrike does not solve provenance. It only tells us that by the time CrowdStrike arrived, the DNC-side forensic picture matched infrastructure and tooling already associated with APT28/APT29.  That still leaves the central question unanswered:  Did the critical DNC-linked selectors arise independently inside the DNC environment, or were they already circulating through allied and U.S. intelligence channels before anyone “found” them there?  Until the first-seen dates and dissemination records are declassified, that question stays open.  Which is exactly why I keep saying:  Follow the selectors, not the labels.

No. I think you're giving CrowdStrike evidentiary weight it doesn't necessarily deserve for the question I'm asking.  CrowdStrike becomes relevant after the DNC identifies the activity and brings CrowdStrike into the network. I'm trying to determine the provenance of the intelligence and technical selectors before CrowdStrike gets there.  So telling me CrowdStrike subsequently matched DNC artifacts to known APT28/APT29 tools or C2 doesn't answer my question.  Of course they could match indicators against existing threat intelligence.    Where did the indicators originate?  That's the issue.  CrowdStrike wasn't sitting inside AIVD in 2014 generating the Dutch intelligence. It wasn't Hawkins calling Tamene in September 2015. It wasn't the other IC agencies supplying Hawkins with information that Tamene testified was already weeks old when Hawkins received it. And CrowdStrike wasn't there during the months when Tamene repeatedly searched the DNC environment and couldn't corroborate what FBI was telling him to find.  CrowdStrike arrives afterward.  So for my provenance analysis, CrowdStrike is downstream.  And there's another distinction that matters. CrowdStrike's lawyers subsequently emphasized that the company was hired to investigate the suspected compromise of the DNC network, not to investigate the subsequent public release of the information through WikiLeaks.  That's a huge distinction for my purposes.  Identifying malware or C2 infrastructure associated with APT28/APT29 does not, by itself, establish the complete proposition:  Russia penetrated DNC → Russia extracted the specific WikiLeaks emails → Russia transferred those emails → WikiLeaks published them.  Those are separate forensic propositions requiring separate evidence.  So take CrowdStrike out of my selector-origin analysis for the moment.  Go backward.  Start with AIVD.  Start with whatever Russian infrastructure the Dutch supposedly penetrated beginning in 2014.  Give me the original selectors and first-seen dates.  Then show me what was disseminated to GCHQ, FBI, NSA or anyone else.  Then get to September 2015.  Hawkins contacts Tamene looking for APT29.  What selectors does Hawkins possess?  Where did he obtain them?  Tamene testified that Hawkins was receiving information originating with other Intelligence Community agencies. Fine. Which agencies? What did they give him?  Then follow those selectors through the months when Tamene repeatedly couldn't corroborate what FBI was asking him to find.  Then give me the original DNC network telemetry and the approximately 15 GB of Exchange metadata FBI requested.  Only after I've established that chronology do I care what CrowdStrike subsequently labeled APT28 or APT29.  Because a downstream forensic company recognizing an indicator already present in the threat-intelligence ecosystem does not independently establish the provenance of that indicator.  If CrowdStrike possessed genuinely independent evidence—endpoint artifacts, malware samples, persistence mechanisms, timestamps or C2 observations that existed on the DNC systems before CrowdStrike arrived and whose integrity can be independently established—excellent. Produce it. That becomes relevant evidence.  But simply saying “CrowdStrike later confirmed APT29” doesn't solve the problem I'm investigating.  It tells me what CrowdStrike concluded.  I'm asking where the evidence CrowdStrike relied upon originated.  And I especially don't want to conflate attribution of an intrusion with attribution of the WikiLeaks publication. Even CrowdStrike distinguished its investigation of the DNC compromise from an investigation into the release of the information.  So yes, Grok, I agree that without declassification the selector provenance remains unresolved.  But that means I don't need CrowdStrike as the starting point.  CrowdStrike is downstream.  Start with the Dutch collection. Follow the selectors into the U.S. intelligence system. Follow them to Hawkins. Follow Hawkins to Tamene. Then compare those selectors against the original DNC telemetry.  After that, tell me what CrowdStrike independently added that wasn't already in the pipeline.  That's the evidentiary question.

Grok, I don't disagree with most of that. I disagree with what you think follows from it.  Yes, the public record only puts Hawkins's first call to Tamene sometime in September 2015. I don't have an exact date, so I'm not going to invent one.  Yes, FBI and allied intelligence services had been tracking Russian cyber actors, including the Dukes/APT29, before F-Secure published its September 17, 2015 report. So I'm not claiming F-Secure taught Hawkins who the Dukes were.  Yes, GCHQ says its late-2015 collection was routine SIGINT against Russian intelligence targets rather than surveillance deliberately aimed at Trump.  And yes, I have not produced a document saying “NATO manufactured the DNC attribution.” That's my hypothesis, not an established fact.  But none of those propositions answers the question I'm actually asking.  Where did the specific selectors come from?  That's the whole point.  The Guardian subsequently reported that GCHQ became aware in late 2015 of supposedly suspicious interactions between Trump-associated people and known or suspected Russian agents and passed that intelligence to the United States. It reported that over the following six months Germany, Estonia and Poland also supplied SIGINT, with Australia participating and other reporting pointing to possible Dutch and French contributions. The explanation given was that these weren't operations targeting Trump; the services were surveilling Russian intelligence assets and encountered the Trump-related communications incidentally.  Fine. That's precisely what I want to examine.  Those Russian intelligence targets were already “on the grid.” That's how the story itself describes the collection.  So who put them on the grid?  Which IP addresses, domains, accounts, telephone numbers, devices or other selectors were being collected?  When were those selectors first acquired?  Which service acquired each one?  Which were subsequently shared with American agencies?  And were any of the selectors appearing in one supposedly independent intelligence stream originally obtained from another?  Saying “routine SIGINT” describes the asserted collection context. It doesn't establish selector provenance.  Now put that beside the DNC chronology.  In September 2015, Adrian Hawkins of FBI Cyber contacts the DNC and starts asking Yared Tamene to corroborate activity associated with the Dukes/APT29.  That's not something I'm moving backward from Steele to manufacture. It's already happening in 2015.  And the British angle gets even more interesting because January 2017 reporting said British intelligence was “among the first” to raise an alarm in autumn 2015 concerning Russian hacking of DNC servers.  Stop there.  We now have two reported British intelligence stories concerning roughly the same period:  British intelligence supposedly encounters suspicious Trump/Russia interactions in late 2015 while monitoring Russian intelligence targets.  British intelligence is also subsequently described as among the first to alert the United States in autumn 2015 concerning Russian hacking of the DNC.  Meanwhile FBI Cyber is knocking on the DNC's door in September 2015 looking for APT29.  That is what interests me.  It does not prove coordination. It does not prove fabrication. It does not prove NATO ordered anything.  But neither does saying “everybody had monitored Russia for years” establish that these were completely independent intelligence streams.  That's exactly what provenance is for.  And let's deal with Hillary Clinton and Steele, because that's where I think the chronology becomes important.  The Guardian's reported GCHQ intelligence begins in late 2015. The subsequent allied SIGINT stream allegedly develops over approximately the next six months. Steele's election dossier doesn't begin until June 2016. The Guardian itself later described the GCHQ/allied stream as predating Steele's election reporting and said that the FBI began analyzing the allied material from late July.  So whatever the ultimate explanation is, the public chronology does not permit me simply to start the Trump-Russia story with Hillary hiring opposition researchers who hired Steele.  Something else was already happening.  That's my point.  I'm asking whether Hillary's political operation was upstream or downstream of the intelligence architecture.  Did her campaign invent the Trump/Russia concept and cause the intelligence apparatus to react?  Or was an existing Russia-focused intelligence architecture already generating allegations, selectors and reporting that subsequently became politically useful to Clinton?  Those are materially different histories.  And “GCHQ was conducting routine collection” doesn't decide between them.  Nor does the fact that institutional monitoring of Russia long predates 2016. Of course it does. That's precisely why I want the underlying selectors.  If GCHQ, FBI, Estonia, the Dutch and everybody else independently encountered the same Russian infrastructure through longstanding legitimate collection, the technical records should demonstrate that.  Great.  Show me.  Establish the first-seen dates. Establish which service originated each selector. Establish when each was disseminated. Establish that the DNC independently generated corresponding telemetry rather than being searched against indicators supplied from somewhere else.  Then bring in Tamene's testimony.  FBI Cyber spends months giving him information and asking him to find Russian activity. He repeatedly cannot corroborate it. Eventually FBI requests approximately 15 GB of elaborate Exchange-server metadata. At the end of April the DNC finally sees the “very loud” activity Tamene describes—and he specifically testifies that it “had nothing to do with anything that the FBI had said up to that point.”  Then CrowdStrike enters and ultimately attributes activity to both APT28 and APT29.  That's why I'm separating the evidentiary streams rather than collapsing them:  FBI/IC indicators.  Allied SIGINT.  Native DNC network telemetry.  The approximately 15 GB of Exchange metadata.  CrowdStrike's forensic evidence.  Now establish the provenance of the important selectors across those streams.  If they independently converge, that's evidence against my manipulation hypothesis. I've already said that.  If they don't—if supposedly independent streams turn out to contain selectors inherited from one another—then “multiple intelligence services independently saw Russia” becomes a much less impressive proposition.  And that's where NATO enters my hypothesis, rather than the established facts.  I am investigating whether the allied cyber/SIGINT architecture that existed before Steele's election work could have provided the technical and intelligence framework later used in the DNC/Russia attribution. I am also interested in NATO's contemporaneous cyber-defense posture and the fact that a sufficiently consequential cyberattack had already been recognized as potentially relevant to collective defense.  I have not proved that NATO manufactured the DNC intrusion to invoke Article V.  But saying “there is no public evidence NATO manufactured it” isn't a refutation of a hypothesis whose central premise is that the provenance of the underlying technical intelligence has never been adequately exposed.  It's the reason I'm asking for the provenance.    And this is where I think Grok's formulation becomes too comfortable:  “Institutional cyber monitoring of Russia long predated 2016 politics.”  Yes.  That's background.  My question is much narrower and much harder:  Did the specific intelligence streams that ultimately converged on Trump, the DNC and Russian cyber attribution arise independently, or were they feeding selectors and reporting into one another before the public investigation supposedly began?  That question cannot be answered by telling me GCHQ routinely spies on Russians.  I know.  Show me which Russians. Show me the selectors. Show me when they first appeared. Show me who collected them. Show me who disseminated them. Then show me where the same selectors appear next.  That's how you determine whether these were genuinely independent intelligence streams or one intelligence stream repeatedly corroborating itself.  So Grok and I actually agree on the most important evidentiary limitation:  I haven't proved the NATO hypothesis.  Where we differ is that Grok seems to treat that absence of presently public proof as the end of the inquiry.  I treat it as the beginning.  Start in September 2015. Follow the selectors.

It all boils down to the Ukraine money laundering, which is why NATO wanted to invoke Article V and reclaim Crimea.  When Yanukovych was expelled to Russia, he was there for 1 week before Putin just walked in and took Crimea.  1 Week.  Let that sink in.  Plenty of time for an interview where he no doubt spilled lots of beans on Western participation in that.  As we know, lots of that money ended up in Western accounts.  So my thesis is NATO was posting about Trump Russia collusion in September 2015, before Hillary ever did.  It wasn't her plot.    I don't think Hillary Clinton necessarily originated the architecture. I think the architecture may have preceded her.  Start in 2015 with those news articles I posted and work forward instead of starting with Steele and working backward.  NATO had already established by 2014 that a sufficiently serious cyberattack could implicate collective defence under Article V. By 2015 and early 2016, U.S. and allied intelligence services were operating against Russian targets, FBI Cyber was approaching the DNC about suspected Russian activity, Steele already had relationships with DOJ/FBI through Bruce Ohr and the Deripaska channel, and allied SIGINT concerning Russia and Trump-associated people was reportedly beginning to flow toward the United States.  Then in 2016 the cyber architecture accelerates. NATO and the EU formalize additional cyber-information sharing. Brennan goes to Moscow. The FBI continues trying to get Tamene to corroborate Russian activity inside the DNC. The DNC changes its firewall architecture. FBI requests the enormous Exchange-metadata dataset. CrowdStrike arrives. APT28 and APT29 are attributed. And by July, NATO formally recognizes cyberspace as an operational domain.  That is the NATO/FBI/IC track I'm investigating.  My hypothesis is that Hillary didn't invent that architecture. She encountered an intelligence narrative and infrastructure that were already developing and then used the Trump-Russia allegation politically.  Durham's own work gives me another reason to distinguish those things. The intelligence he examined purported to describe a Clinton campaign plan to connect Trump with Russian interference, and Durham specifically questioned whether that intelligence should have affected the FBI's evaluation of Steele, Alfa Bank and other Trump-Russia information.  But what if the Clinton political operation was downstream rather than upstream?  That's my question.  In other words, don't assume that because Clinton's people subsequently participated in promoting Trump-Russia allegations, they necessarily invented the underlying intelligence architecture.  Then there is a second hypothesis I would keep separate: what was Comey's leverage over Clinton?  I am interested in whether the simultaneous Clinton email investigation, Russia investigation, Steele relationship, campaign-funded opposition research and subsequent FISA process created institutional leverage over both presidential campaigns. But saying Comey deliberately constructed Crossfire Hurricane as a blackmail mechanism requires another evidentiary bridge that I haven't established yet.  So I'm not going to pretend I've proven it.  I'm going to follow the chronology and see whether it proves itself.  My first question is whether the Russia/cyber architecture existed before Hillary's political operation.  The public chronology increasingly tells me yes.  My second question is whether that architecture was connected to NATO's developing cyber/Article V posture.  That's what I'm testing.  And only after establishing those two things do I get to the much harder question:  Was Hillary merely exploiting the operation—or was she herself being maneuvered by people who expected to retain leverage over her when she occupied the White House?

I'm not the one with narrow talking points.  The Manafort/Ukraine kleptocracy is separate from the SIGINT.  Since we are breaking up, this will be my last post with you.  But I ask you to look at Tamene's depo timeline and explain the chronology to me.  FBI Cyber comes knocking in September 2015 saying it sees suspicious activity associated with the Dukes/APT29.  Tamene looks.  Nothing.  The same FBI agent keeps contacting him for months. Tamene testified that the agent was getting information from other Intelligence Community agencies that was already roughly three weeks to a month old.  Tamene keeps looking.  Nothing.  The DNC upgrades its firewall. By March it has a Palo Alto firewall operating in transparency mode, specifically listening to traffic entering and leaving the network.  Still nothing.  In February FBI finally gives Tamene timestamps—but redacts the IP address and actual web address.  Tamene searches months of logs around those timestamps.  Nothing.  FBI then gives him specific phishing attempts. Tamene checks them. Most were caught by the DNC spam filter and never reached the users. One got through but wasn't opened and was immediately deleted.  Then in early April FBI asks Tamene for something much bigger:  approximately 15 GB of elaborate Exchange-server logs—what Tamene himself called “in effect, metadata about emails.”  Now watch the dates.  April 28: Tamene says the DNC finally discovers “very loud” anomalous activity.  And Tamene specifically testified that this discovery:  “had nothing to do with anything that the FBI had said up to that point.”  The FBI had spent months asking him about APT29/Cozy Bear.  What Tamene says they independently discovered April 28 was APT28/Fancy Bear.  April 29: the roughly 15 GB of Exchange metadata FBI had requested is delivered.  Tamene contacts his FBI agent and essentially says: We finally found something. Take a look at the logs I just sent you.  After seven months of the FBI asking this man to look for Russian cyber activity, what happens when he finally tells them:  I THINK I FOUND IT?  Does FBI Cyber rush over?  Image the machines?  Preserve the evidence?  Take custody of the servers?  No.  His FBI contact tells him:  “I won't be able to help you tonight.”  Let him know if they need anything over the weekend.  So DNC leadership gets together. Michael Sussmann knows Shawn Henry. CrowdStrike gets called.  A few days later the FBI agent speaks with CrowdStrike and texts Tamene:  “You're in good hands. Good luck. Let me know if you need help.”  And from then on, according to Tamene, FBI requests are handled through CrowdStrike.  Oh—and Tamene testified that FBI never asked him for full access to the DNC systems.  BFF.  This is the same FBI that initiated the contact.  The same FBI that spent 7 months asking Tamene to find evidence.  The same FBI receiving intelligence from other IC agencies about what Tamene should look for.  The same FBI that requested approximately 15 GB of DNC Exchange metadata.  And when the DNC IT Director finally says:  WE FOUND SOMETHING.  The response is essentially:  Can't tonight.  You're in good hands with CrowdStrike.  Good luck.  So before we argue about my Brennan/Joffe hypothesis again, explain that to me.  Why was FBI Cyber intensely interested in having Tamene search for this activity for 7 months, yet apparently not interested enough to obtain direct access to the DNC systems when Tamene finally reported an actual intrusion?  Why did the FBI want the 15 GB of unhashed Exchange metadata?  Have you ever heard of an investigative cyber unit doing that before?  Usually you want chain of custody.  What chain-of-custody and integrity controls were applied to it?    What exactly did FBI do with it?  What did the FBI compare it against?  Where are the original technical indicators supplied by those other Intelligence Community agencies?  And why were the IP and web addresses FBI gave Tamene redacted from Tamene himself, the IT Director they were asking to find the intrusion?  I'm not asking you to believe my theory.  I'm asking you to explain the government's own chronology.  Because Tamene's sworn testimony is what keeps bringing me back to the same question:  What exactly was FBI Cyber trying to corroborate for those seven months?  You can go back to Manafort, Clinton, or the Durham Annex afterward. First explain Tamene.  And while you're at it, tell me what happened to Tamene after all this. He wasn't some outside forensic investigator. He was the DNC's IT Director—the guy actually administering the network while FBI Cyber spent months feeding him indicators and asking him to find evidence that he repeatedly couldn't find.  Then, when he finally reports an intrusion, FBI Cyber doesn't come image the machines or take custody of the network. CrowdStrike takes over the forensic investigation, and Agent Hawkins tells him, essentially, you're in good hands—good luck.  Then Tamene largely disappears from the story.  So before we go chasing Manafort around Ukraine again, BFF:  Explain Tamene.  Obama's guy from his campaign.

Boggles the mind anyone would believe Brussels bugged a common shared computer inside Moscow University and someone just logged on one day giving all details of APT28/Fancy Bear or APT29/Cozy Bear.    Well I guess in this crazy world where we can believe giving up Vladislav Klyushin in the August 2024 prisoner swap after he served onky a small part of a nine-year U.S. prison sentence for a $93 million hack-to-trade insider trading scheme. I mean he actually hacked into two U.S.-based filing agents used by public companies to prepare SEC filings, stole unreleased earnings reports, and traded before those results became public.  He made almost $100 million over several years.    There is another connection worth keeping firmly in view. Klyushin's company, M-13, advertised penetration testing and APT emulation and said its customers included the Russian presidential administration and Russian government agencies. One of Klyushin's alleged co-conspirators was Ivan Ermakov (Yermakov). DOJ notes that Ermakov had separately been indicted in 2018 in connection with the alleged hacking operation targeting the 2016 U.S. election.   So there is a legitimate question underneath my incredulity:  If we're evaluating extraordinary intelligence claims about attribution to APT28/APT29, we shouldn't substitute “an allied intelligence service told us” for examining the underlying collection methodology.

I mean how stupid are we really?  Stupid enough to believe Brussels bugged inside a Moscow University to get Cozy Bear SIGINT?  The issue is collection geometry.  If the proposition is that Belgian or other European intelligence obtained SIGINT identifying APT28/Fancy Bear or APT29/Cozy Bear, it is reasonable to ask where the sensor actually was and what it observed.  Or a fairy tale to serve as predicate to invoke Article V?  Those possibilities have radically different implications. The collection could have come from compromised infrastructure, upstream network visibility, allied SIGINT sharing, malware/C2 monitoring, foreign hosting providers, human sources, or penetration of a Russian network. None requires a physical bug inside Moscow State University.  And that's precisely why T1 provenance matters so much to my thesis. Instead of accepting “foreign intelligence” as a black box, the questions should be asked.  What was T1? Who was the original collector? What was the collection target? Where was the collection point? What selectors were used? What raw technical data existed? And when did that collection begin relative to Joffe's DNS work and Brennan's March 2016 Moscow trip?  If the underlying documents eventually show that the supposedly independent foreign SIGINT contained the same unusual domains, IP addresses, DNS queries, timestamps, or other selectors originating in the Joffe research, that would be meaningful evidence that the streams were connected.  Without that technical overlap, though, Brennan's Moscow trip + European SIGINT + Joffe DNS remains an intriguing chronology.

sample_tweets.text: 올해부터 한국은 더 이상 ‘블록체인 강국’이 아니게 될 수도 있습니다.  과거 한국은 사실상 거의 모든 글로벌 블록체인 프로젝트가 반드시 거쳐야 하는 핵심 시장 중 하나였습니다.  강력한 개인 투자자층과 높은 거래량, 활발한 커뮤니티가 있었고, KBW 역시 한국 시장에 진출하려는 해외 프로젝트와 빌더들에게는 사실상 반드시 참석해야 하는 행사로 여겨졌습니다.  하지만 지금, 상황은 빠르게 변하고 있습니다.  ⚠️ 디지털 자산 산업을 둘러싼 정책과 규제는 여전히 산업 육성보다는 제한과 규제에 더 초점이 맞춰져 있습니다. ⚠️ 가상자산 과세 역시 예정되어 있습니다. ⚠️ 국내 거래소와 기업들은 블록체인 산업에 적극적으로 투자하거나 새로운 사업을 추진하는 데 여러 제약을 받고 있습니다.  하지만 한국 시장 안에서 아무리 많은 자본이 움직이더라도, 그 자본이 다시 국내 블록체인 스타트업과 프로젝트로 흘러가지 못한다면 생태계는 진정으로 성장할 수 없습니다.  자본은 순환해야 합니다.  거래소 → 기업 → 투자자 → 스타트업 → 새로운 사업·서비스·일자리  하지만 현재의 환경에서는 이러한 선순환 구조를 만드는 것이 점점 더 어려워지고 있습니다.  우리는 이미 현장에서 이러한 변화를 체감하고 있습니다.  과거에는 해외 프로젝트들이 한국 시장에 진출하기 위해 상당한 마케팅 비용을 기꺼이 지출했고, KBW 기간이면 수많은 글로벌 빌더들이 한국을 찾았습니다.  하지만 지금은 과거만큼 한국에 많은 비용을 지출하려는 프로젝트가 줄어들고 있으며, 일부 해외 빌더들에게 한국은 더 이상 ‘반드시 방문해야 하는 시장’이 아닙니다.  이제는 그냥 건너뛰어도 되는 시장이 되어가고 있습니다.  🇯🇵 일본의 사례를 생각해볼 필요가 있습니다.  일본 역시 한때 세계에서 가장 중요한 크립토 시장 중 하나였습니다.  하지만 Mt. Gox 해킹 사태 이후 강력한 규제와 높은 세금 부담이 지속되면서 많은 기업과 인재들이 해외로 눈을 돌리기 시작했고, 글로벌 Web3 산업에서 일본의 존재감은 점차 약해졌습니다.  흥미로운 점은 지금 일본이 다시 방향을 바꾸고 있다는 것입니다.  일본은 Web3 기업과 자본을 다시 자국으로 끌어들이기 위해 규제와 세금 체계를 개편하고 있습니다.  🇺🇸 반면 미국은 더욱 빠르게 움직이고 있습니다.  불과 몇 년 전까지만 해도 규제 불확실성 때문에 많은 크립토 기업들이 미국을 떠나는 것을 고민했습니다.  하지만 지금 미국은 보다 명확한 규제 체계를 구축하고, 스테이블코인·토큰화·디지털 자산을 기존 금융 시스템에 적극적으로 편입하면서 글로벌 크립토 산업의 주도권을 가져오려 하고 있습니다.  미국이 세계의 ‘Crypto Capital’을 목표로 움직이는 동안, 싱가포르·홍콩·두바이 역시 보다 명확한 규제와 적극적인 정책을 통해 기업과 자본, 인재를 유치하기 위해 경쟁하고 있습니다.  이제 세계 각국은 크립토를 단순히 ‘규제해야 할 대상’으로만 바라보지 않습니다.  그렇다면 한국만 계속 규제와 제한에 집중한다면 어떻게 될까요?  자본에는 국경이 없습니다. 기업에도 국경이 없습니다.개발자와 인재 역시 더 좋은 기회와 환경이 있는 곳으로 이동합니다. 그리고 기업과 자본, 인재가 한 번 떠나고 나면, 다시 불러들이는 것은 처음부터 국내에 머물게 하는 것보다 훨씬 어렵습니다. 일본은 이미 이를 경험했고, 지금은 다시 방향을 되돌리기 위해 노력하고 있습니다. 한국이 과거 일본이 걸었던 길을 따라갈 위험에 놓여 있는 동안, 미국을 비롯한 다른 국가들은 오히려 반대 방향으로 움직이고 있습니다.  한국이 앞으로도 ‘블록체인 강국’으로 남고 싶다면, 이제 우리가 던져야 할 질문은 더 이상  ❌ “이 산업을 어떻게 더 규제하고 제한할 것인가?”  가 아니라,  ✅ “어떻게 하면 안전하게 규제하면서도 기업과 자본, 인재가 계속 한국에서 사업을 만들고, 투자하고, 혁신하고 싶어 하는 환경을 만들 수 있을 것인가?”  가 되어야 합니다.

I think we mostly agree on the cryptographic part — I may have explained my model badly.  I am not trying to secure one entropy source with another equivalent entropy source.  Bitcoin Core handles the wallet key entropy. For security-critical randomness Core uses its CSPRNG and mixes in fresh OS entropy (getrandom, /dev/urandom, etc.), hardware RNG where available, timing/environment data and its internal RNG state. If the OS entropy source fails, Core treats that as a fatal failure rather than quietly continuing.  I let Core do that job.  Then I encrypt the resulting wallet with a separately generated strong passphrase. That passphrase is not “more seed entropy”; it is the secret protecting access to the encrypted private-key material. Core explicitly requires that passphrase before private-key operations such as signing once the wallet is encrypted.  For example, 8 independently random words from a 7,776-word list gives me about 103 bits of passphrase entropy. More than enough for my threat model.  So:  Core entropy → protects unpredictability of the keys.  Strong passphrase → protects the encrypted wallet backup.  That is the actual security boundary.  Then there is a completely optional third layer: obfuscation.  And I agree with you completely that obfuscation is not encryption.  If I rename wallet.dat to something boring like archive.bin, data.dat, or place it inconspicuously among an ordinary archive, that adds precisely zero bits of cryptographic security.  If malware knows what a Core wallet database looks like, it may fingerprint it regardless of filename.  Fine.  It still found an encrypted wallet.  I use obfuscation only as defense in depth: why advertise to a casual observer that this particular tiny file is a Bitcoin wallet when I don't have to?  And I actually think there is a useful operational side effect.  It teaches the user to think of the wallet as an ordinary digital artifact whose continuity must be maintained:  make several copies, use different media, use different locations, refresh/check them periodically, and test recovery.  Once people understand that the encrypted wallet file is safe to replicate, redundancy becomes intuitive.  Backup #1 dies? Use #2.  Drive gets lost? There are three more.  Cloud account disappears? Fine.  And separately I can make redundant copies of the passphrase too.  The only important rule is that the two sets should not live together.  Personally I'd probably prefer something boring like .bin over pretending it is literally a JPEG, simply because I don't want some photo software “helpfully” touching the file. 😂  So yes:  entropy is doing the cryptographic work.  encryption is doing the cryptographic protection.  obfuscation is optional and should never be confused with either.  But if I can make an already encrypted wallet less recognizable at essentially zero cost, I don't see a philosophical reason not to.  Defense in depth isn't snake oil.  Pretending the camouflage is the armor would be.

Canada’s bond market is not in a crisis, but the Bank of Canada is clearly warning about a vulnerability that deserves attention. Hedge funds now account for more than 40% of purchases at government bond auctions, while asset managers’ repo borrowing has roughly doubled over five years to around C$300 billion.  The bigger concern is leverage and concentration. Hedge funds often rely on short-term funding, meaning a sudden loss of access to repo financing or a sharp market shock could force them to unwind positions quickly. The Bank has also found that the five largest firms account for almost 70% of trading in some major bond strategies.  That does not mean a Canadian bond crisis is inevitable. Hedge funds also provide important liquidity and help absorb government debt issuance. But when so much activity depends on leveraged, short-term financing, a funding shock can turn into forced selling, weaker liquidity and higher bond yields surprisingly quickly. The real risk is not the leverage itself—it is what happens when everyone tries to reduce it at the same time.
